docs.title: verdance
docs.text:
Measure the 3-30-300 rule of urban greening for any city, powered by Apache Sedona.

The 3-30-300 rule (Konijnendijk, 2023) states that every home should:

  1. See at least 3 trees — the number of trees within a buffer of each building (T3), or the number visible from its windows (Visibility),
  2. Sit in a neighbourhood with at least 30 % canopy cover (T30),
  3. Be within 300 m of a public green space (T300).

verdance computes each metric per building and per census unit from standard geospatial inputs — or from global open data (Overture Maps, OpenStreetMap, the Meta/WRI canopy height model) where local data is missing — evaluates the rule for every building, merges everything into one analysis-ready table, and serves an interactive map of the results.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
pip install verdance

verdance runs on Python 3.12+ and needs a Java 11–17 runtime for Spark. See Installation for the Java setup, the optional extras and the Docker image.

docs.title: A city in one config file
docs.text:
A study area is described by one YAML file. The smallest useful config needs only census boundaries of your own — one polygon per unit, with a column for each level of the hierarchy — and takes everything else from global open data:

# mycity.yaml
study_area_name: MyCity
crs: EPSG:32630                   # a projected CRS in metres covering the city

data:
  census_boundaries: /path/to/wards.gpkg
  buildings: overture             # Overture Maps footprints
  parks_sites: overture           # Overture parks and recreation grounds
  parks_access: osm               # OSM entrances
  roads: osm                      # OSM walking network
  meta_chm: v1                    # Meta/WRI 1 m canopy height from AWS: the "30"
  trees_dir: /path/to/output/trees   # filled by `-p Trees`: the "3"

tree_segmentation:
  source: meta
  preset: meta

park_min_area_ha: 0.5             # ignore green spaces under 0.5 ha (WHO guidance)

columns:
  geo_levels: [district_code, ward_code]   # coarsest → finest

output:
  base_dir: /path/to/output

Then run the modules one at a time, Merge last, and open the map:

verdance validate -c mycity.yaml                      # check the config before a long run
verdance run -c mycity.yaml -p Trees                  # segment tree crowns from the CHM
verdance run -c mycity.yaml -p T3 --buffer 50         # trees within 50 m of each building
verdance run -c mycity.yaml -p T30                    # canopy cover per ward
verdance run -c mycity.yaml -p T300                   # distance to the nearest park
verdance run -c mycity.yaml -p Tree_count
verdance run -c mycity.yaml -p Merge --t3_buffers 50  # the rule per building and per unit
verdance viz -c mycity.yaml                           # interactive map at localhost:8765

The results are database/T3_30_300_buildings.parquet (one row per building, with meets_3, meets_30, meets_300 and meets_3_30_300) and database/T3_30_300_spectral.parquet (one row per unit, with the share of buildings meeting each criterion).

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Each study area is described by a YAML config. examples/generic.yaml is a fully commented template of every key, and the reference below is generated from the config schema itself.

More examples live in examples/: osm.yaml (every layer from OpenStreetMap), open_buildings.yaml (Google Open Buildings), nairobi.yaml (a whole city on global open data: Overture buildings and parks, OSM roads, Meta canopy height, global building heights) and UK setups with local data (westminster.yaml, anglesey.yaml, england.yaml). Their paths point to the author's machines: replace them with yours.

The key sections:

study_area_name: MyCity
crs: EPSG:32632          # projected CRS in metres

data:                    # paths to the inputs below
  buildings: /path/to/buildings.gpkg   # or "osm" / "overture" / "open_buildings"
  trees_dir: /path/to/trees/
  chm_tiles_dir: null    # alternative to trees_dir for T30
  ...

columns:                 # your column names → verdance's canonical names
  building_id: building_id
  tree_height_col: height
  tree_area_col: area
  geo_levels:            # geography hierarchy, coarsest → finest
    - district_code
    - tract_code

output:
  base_dir: /path/to/output/

Check a config before a long run

verdance validate -c mycity.yaml is a dry run that checks input files, geo-level columns, CRS and Java, so a typo fails in seconds rather than part-way through Spark.

docs.title: Input data
docs.text:
All inputs are vector files readable by GeoPandas (GeoPackage, Shapefile, GeoJSON, (Geo)Parquet…).

  • Census boundaries (required, always a file) — one polygon per unit of the finest geography, with a column for every level of the hierarchy (e.g. district and tract codes). They define the study area, including where remote layers are fetched.
  • Buildings — footprint polygons with a unique id column (columns.building_id). Instead of a file, data.buildings also accepts osm (OpenStreetMap; height and building:levels tags are kept where mapped), overture (Overture Maps, global; height and num_floors are kept but sparse outside major cities), or open_buildings (Google Open Buildings v3 via GEE, needs gee_project; no heights, and covers Africa, South/Southeast Asia and Latin America & the Caribbean only — not Europe or North America). Visibility also needs building heights, which the Heights process attaches from global datasets when the footprints have none — see Building heights.
  • Trees — canopy polygons with height and area attributes (a single file or a directory of tiles), or segment them from a CHM with the Trees process — see Tree segmentation.
  • Canopy for T30 — one of: a directory of CHM raster tiles (.tif, chm_tiles_dir); the Meta/WRI global canopy height model from AWS (meta_chm: v1 or v2, no account needed); a GEE canopy-height asset (canopy_height_ee_path, needs gee_project); or the tree polygons above. See Canopy cover source.
  • Parks — green-space polygons, plus access points (can be the same file), or osm / overture (parks) and osm (access points). Set park_min_area_ha to ignore small green spaces — the WHO guideline behind the 300 rule uses ≥ 0.5–1 ha. Access points are only filtered along with their parks when columns.park_access_ref_col links them.
  • Roads — edges (and optionally nodes; nodes are derived from edge endpoints if absent), or osm. File-based networks must be noded (split at every intersection) and reduced to their largest connected component, or buildings snapping to isolated fragments get null network distances. columns.road_edge_length should hold edge lengths in metres; if the column is missing, lengths are computed from the geometry in the config CRS, with a warning.

On the first run, verdance converts everything to a parquet cache in <output.base_dir>/database/, renaming your columns to canonical names. Delete that folder to rebuild the cache after changing input data or column mappings.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text:
Generated from verdance.config.schema. Every key below is a YAML key in the config file; nested sections map to the dataclasses that follow.

A complete verdance study-area configuration, loaded from YAML by verdance.load_config.

examples/generic.yaml is a fully commented template of every key below.

Source code in src/verdance/config/schema.py 
@dataclass
class VerdanceConfig:
    """A complete verdance study-area configuration, loaded from YAML by
    `verdance.load_config`.

    `examples/generic.yaml` is a fully commented template of every key below.
    """

    study_area_name: str
    """Name of the study area, used in output filenames and the viz title."""
    crs: str
    """Projected CRS in metres that every layer is reprojected to, e.g. `EPSG:32632`.
    A geographic CRS is rejected: the buffers and areas verdance computes are metric."""
    data: DataPaths
    """Input layers: where each one is read from."""
    columns: ColumnMapping
    """Which column of each input layer holds each value verdance needs."""
    output: OutputPaths
    """Where results and caches are written."""
    gee_project: str | None = None
    """Google Earth Engine project, required by the GEE-backed sources (Spectral,
    GEE canopy and building heights, and terrain for Visibility). Authenticate once
    with `earthengine authenticate`."""
    gee_boundaries_asset: str | None = None
    """GEE table asset of the census boundaries — Spectral only."""
    park_min_area_ha: float | None = None
    """Drop parks smaller than this many hectares before T300; None keeps all. The WHO
    guideline behind the 300 rule uses green spaces of at least 0.5-1 ha."""
    dggs: str | None = None
    """Aggregate to discrete global grid cells instead of the finest geo level:
    `h3`, `s2`, `geohash`, `a5` or `rhealpix`."""
    dggs_resolution: int | None = None
    """Resolution of the `dggs` grid; its meaning depends on the system chosen."""
    h3_resolution: int | None = None
    """Deprecated: use `dggs: h3` with `dggs_resolution`. The loader normalizes it there."""
    tile_system: TileSystemConfig = field(default_factory=TileSystemConfig)
    """Legacy UK VOM tile settings, parsed so older configs still load."""
    osm: OSMConfig = field(default_factory=OSMConfig)
    """Options for layers with their data path set to `osm`."""
    open_buildings: OpenBuildingsConfig = field(default_factory=OpenBuildingsConfig)
    """Options for buildings set to `open_buildings`."""
    overture: OvertureConfig = field(default_factory=OvertureConfig)
    """Options for layers set to `overture`."""
    tree_segmentation: TreeSegmentationConfig = field(default_factory=TreeSegmentationConfig)
    """Options for the Trees process."""
    heights: HeightsConfig = field(default_factory=HeightsConfig)
    """Options for the Heights process, and the building heights Visibility uses."""
    visibility: VisibilityConfig = field(default_factory=VisibilityConfig)
    """Options for the Visibility process."""
    terrain: TerrainConfig = field(default_factory=TerrainConfig)
    """Ground elevation under buildings and trees, for raster Visibility."""
    context_buffer: float = 100.0
    """Metres around the study area from which context is gathered: buildings that
    block views (Visibility) and trees that count for edge buildings (Trees, so T3
    and Visibility)."""

docs.title: DataPaths dataclass
docs.text:
Where each input layer is read from: a file path, or a remote source name.

Source code in src/verdance/config/schema.py 
@dataclass
class DataPaths:
    """Where each input layer is read from: a file path, or a remote source name."""

    buildings: str
    """Building footprints: a file path, or one of `osm`, `overture`, `open_buildings`."""
    parks_sites: str
    """Park polygons: a file path, or `osm` / `overture`."""
    parks_access: str
    """Park access points: a file path, or `osm`."""
    roads: str
    """Road edges: a file path, or `osm`."""
    census_boundaries: str
    """Census unit boundaries, carrying every column named in `columns.geo_levels`."""
    road_nodes: str | None = None
    """Road nodes, when the road network is split across two files."""
    trees_dir: str | None = None
    """Directory of segmented tree crowns — written by `Trees`, read by T3 and Tree_count."""
    chm_tiles_dir: str | None = None
    """Directory of canopy height model tiles. Suits survey tiles; globally-tiled
    models belong in `meta_chm`, which reads only the boundary window."""
    chm_pattern: str = "*.tif"
    """Glob for CHM tiles under `chm_tiles_dir` (searched recursively), used by T30,
    T30_buildings and Trees. Defra VOM hillshades (`VOM_HS_*`) are always skipped."""
    chm_overlap: str = "latest"
    """How overlapping CHM tiles (e.g. survey years) combine, for T30, T30_buildings
    and Trees: `latest` takes the last path in sorted order (the latest year for
    `<dir>/<year>/` layouts); `max` takes the per-pixel maximum across them, so a
    tree seen in any survey counts."""
    chm_cache_dir: str | None = None
    """Where downloaded CHM tiles, raster indexes, VRTs and overlap composites go.
    None uses `$VERDANCE_CACHE_DIR`, else `<output.base_dir>/database/chm_cache`."""
    canopy_height_ee_path: str | None = None
    """Google Earth Engine canopy-height asset, e.g.
    `projects/sat-io/open-datasets/facebook/meta-canopy-height`."""
    meta_chm: str | None = None
    """Meta/WRI global 1 m CHM release from the public AWS bucket, `v1` or `v2`.
    When set it is the canopy source of T30 and T30_buildings (after
    `chm_tiles_dir`, before `canopy_height_ee_path`), and the release used wherever
    the `meta` CHM source is read (Trees, raster Visibility); None there means v1."""

docs.title: ColumnMapping dataclass
docs.text:
Which column of each input layer holds each value verdance needs.

Source code in src/verdance/config/schema.py 
@dataclass
class ColumnMapping:
    """Which column of each input layer holds each value verdance needs."""

    building_id: str | None = None
    """Unique building identifier column. Required only when buildings come from a file."""
    building_layer: str | None = None
    """Layer name to read from a multi-layer buildings file."""
    building_height_col: str | None = None
    """Building height in metres (file sources) — read by the "native" height source."""
    building_use_col: str | None = None
    """Keep only buildings whose value here matches `building_use_value`. File-based
    sources only; OSM uses `osm.building_types` instead."""
    building_use_value: str | list[str] | None = None
    """Value, or list of values, of `building_use_col` to keep."""

    road_node_id: str = "id"
    """Unique road-node identifier column."""
    road_edge_start: str = "start_node"
    """Road-edge column holding the id of the node the edge starts at."""
    road_edge_end: str = "end_node"
    """Road-edge column holding the id of the node the edge ends at."""
    road_edge_length: str = "length"
    """Road-edge column holding the edge length in metres."""
    road_edge_layer: str = "road_link"
    """Layer name holding the road edges."""
    road_node_layer: str = "road_node"
    """Layer name holding the road nodes."""

    park_id: str = "id"
    """Unique park identifier column."""
    park_function_col: str | None = None
    """Park column naming the site's function, used to keep only public green space."""
    park_function_value: str | None = None
    """Value of `park_function_col` to keep."""
    park_access_ref_col: str | None = None
    """Access-point column referencing the park it belongs to (joins to `park_id`)."""

    tree_height_col: str = "height"
    """Tree column holding crown height in metres."""
    tree_area_col: str = "area"
    """Tree column holding crown area in square metres."""
    tree_id_col: str = "treeID"
    """Unique tree identifier column."""
    tree_layer: str = "trees"
    """Layer name holding the tree crowns."""

    geo_levels: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    """Census geography columns, ordered coarsest to finest,
    e.g. `["RGN22CD", "LAD22CD", "LSOA21CD", "OA21CD"]`."""
    geo_level_labels: dict[str, str] = field(default_factory=dict)
    """Display names for the levels, e.g. `{ADM3_code: Ward}` — used by the viz."""
    geo_level_names: dict[str, str] = field(default_factory=dict)
    """Per level, a `census_boundaries` column holding each unit's name,
    e.g. `{ADM3_code: ADM3_name}` — used by the viz."""

@dataclass
class OSMConfig:
    """Options for layers sourced from OSM (data paths set to "osm")."""

    network_type: str = "walk"
    """osmnx network type for roads (walkable by default)."""
    building_types: list[str] | None = None
    """`building=*` tag values to fetch. None uses residential defaults;
    `["all"]` takes every building."""
    park_tags: dict[str, list[str]] | None = None
    """OSM tags identifying parks, e.g. `{leisure: [park], landuse: [village_green]}`.
    None uses public-park defaults."""
    exclude_private: bool = True
    """Drop parks tagged `access=private`, `no` or `customers`."""
    fetch_buffer: int = 2000
    """Buffer in metres around the census boundary when fetching roads, parks and
    access points, so the network can route to parks just outside the study area."""

docs.title: Development
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/sdgresearch/verdance.git && cd verdance
uv sync                                   # project environment in .venv, with the dev tools
uv run pytest                             # ~240 tests, about a minute and a half (Spark tests need Java)

uv sync installs into .venv in the repository; to use an environment elsewhere, activate it and pass --active (uv sync --active, uv add --active <package>).

End-to-end check. scripts/make_synthetic_city.py writes a small synthetic city (48 buildings, trees, parks, roads, a CHM and two census levels) and a config for it, so every module can run in a few minutes without downloads:

python scripts/make_synthetic_city.py /tmp/verdance_synth
verdance run -c /tmp/verdance_synth/config.yaml -p T3 --buffer 50   # likewise T30, T300, Tree_count, Visibility, ...
verdance run -c /tmp/verdance_synth/config.yaml -p Merge --t3_buffers 50

The other scripts in scripts/ prepare inputs for particular cities and evaluate tree segmentation and building heights against reference data.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
The site at https://sdgresearch.github.io/verdance/ is built with MkDocs Material from docs/. The config and API references are generated from the source by mkdocstrings, so editing a docstring updates the site.

The docs toolchain is a separate dependency group, installed without the project itself — mkdocstrings reads the package statically, so building the site needs neither Spark, GDAL nor Java:

uv sync --only-group docs
uv run --only-group docs mkdocs serve    # live preview at http://127.0.0.1:8000
uv run --only-group docs mkdocs build --strict   # what CI runs

--strict turns broken links, missing anchors and unresolved API references into errors. Run it before pushing: the docs workflow builds on every pull request that touches docs/, mkdocs.yml or src/, and deploys to the gh-pages branch when master moves.

Pages under docs/superpowers/ are internal design documents and are excluded from the published site.

docs.title: Releasing
docs.text:
Releases are published to PyPI by GitHub Actions through trusted publishing, so no API token is stored anywhere. To cut one:

  1. Bump __version__ in src/verdance/__init__.py — [tool.hatch.version] reads it from there, so it is the only place the version is set.
  2. Move the [Unreleased] section of CHANGELOG.md under the new version number.
  3. Open a pull request, and once it is merged tag the merge commit and push the tag:
git tag -a v<version> -m "v<version>" && git push upstream v<version>

The tag triggers .github/workflows/release.yml, which builds the sdist and wheel and uploads them. To check a build locally first:

rm -rf dist && uv build                   # dist/verdance-<version>.tar.gz and .whl
uvx twine check --strict dist/*

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
verdance needs Python 3.12 or 3.13 and Java 11–17 (Spark 3.5 runs on Java 17 at most; newer Java versions fail).

pip install verdance          # or: uv pip install verdance / uv tool install verdance / pipx install verdance
verdance --version

docs.title: Java
docs.text:
Install a JDK 17 and make sure java -version reports it, or point JAVA_HOME at it:

sudo apt install openjdk-17-jre-headless          # Debian / Ubuntu
brew install openjdk@17                           # macOS (then follow brew's note to link it)
conda install -c conda-forge openjdk=17           # any OS, inside a conda environment
export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-17-openjdk-amd64   # if another Java is the default

The first Spark-based run downloads the Sedona jars (~110 MB, once) into Spark's Ivy cache (~/.ivy2, or VERDANCE_IVY_DIR), so it needs internet access.

No Java at hand?

Use the Docker image, which bundles Java and the jars.

docs.title: Google Earth Engine (optional)
docs.text:
Some data sources are read from Earth Engine: the Spectral module, canopy_height_ee_path, data.buildings: open_buildings, the remote building-height sources and terrain for Visibility. They need a Google Cloud project with Earth Engine enabled: authenticate once with earthengine authenticate (installed with verdance) and set gee_project: <your-project> in the config.

Everything else — including the global open-data sources Overture, OpenStreetMap and the Meta canopy height model from AWS — needs no account.

docs.title: Settings from a .env file
docs.text:
verdance reads a .env file in the working directory (or a parent directory) at startup; variables already set in the environment win. Every setting is optional:

JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-17-openjdk-amd64   # or JDK_HOME, see below
VERDANCE_CACHE_DIR=/big/disk/verdance_cache    # shared download cache
GEE_PROJECT_NAME=my-gee-project                # Earth Engine project when the config has no gee_project

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text:
Variable Meaning JAVA_HOME The Java 11–17 installation Spark runs on. JDK_HOME takes precedence: an absolute path, or the name of a JDK directory under ~/.jdk/ (the layout of the install-jdk package) SPARK_DRIVER_MEMORY Spark's heap (e.g. 16g). Spark runs locally, so this is the memory for all its work. Default: three quarters of the machine's RAM, at most 64g GEE_PROJECT_NAME Earth Engine project used when the config has no gee_project VERDANCE_CACHE_DIR Shared download cache for canopy tiles, Earth Engine rasters and OSM responses VERDANCE_IVY_DIR Where the Sedona/Spark jars are cached VERDANCE_DUCKDB_EXTENSIONS Where the DuckDB spatial extension is cached VERDANCE_SPARK_MASTER Spark master URL; defaults to local[*] TMPDIR Temporary files, including Spark shuffle and spill (SPARK_LOCAL_DIRS overrides it for shuffle files)

Where each of these lands by default is covered in where files go.

docs.title: Docker
docs.text:
The image bundles Python 3.12, OpenJDK 17, the Sedona jars and DuckDB's spatial extension, so it runs without Java installed and without network access for them. Build it from a clone of the repository:

git clone https://github.com/sdgresearch/verdance.git && cd verdance
docker build -t verdance .
docker run --rm verdance --version

Mount a project directory holding the config, the inputs and the output folder, and use container paths in the config (e.g. census_boundaries: /work/data/wards.gpkg, base_dir: /work/output). The image's entrypoint is verdance, so pass only its arguments:

docker run --rm --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" \
  -v "$PWD":/work \
  verdance run -c /work/mycity.yaml -p T3 --buffer 50

--user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" makes the output files yours on a standard Docker install. With rootless Docker use --user 0:0 instead: there the container's root is you, while any other user maps to a host ID you can't write as. Docker Desktop needs neither. To keep downloads between containers, add a cache mount: -v "$HOME/verdance_cache":/cache -e VERDANCE_CACHE_DIR=/cache.

  • Memory. The image defaults to SPARK_DRIVER_MEMORY=4g; raise it on a bigger host with -e SPARK_DRIVER_MEMORY=32g.
  • Earth Engine. Authenticate once on the host (earthengine authenticate), then mount the credentials: -v "$HOME/.config/earthengine":/home/verdance/.config/earthengine:ro, and set gee_project in the config.
  • The map. Publish the port and listen on all interfaces inside the container: docker run --rm -p 8765:8765 -v "$PWD":/work verdance viz -c /work/mycity.yaml --host 0.0.0.0 --no-browser, then open http://localhost:8765.
  • docker compose. docker-compose.yml mounts ./data at /data, ./config at /config and ./output at /output (set output.base_dir: /output), and keeps a download cache in ./cache: docker compose run --rm verdance run -c /config/mycity.yaml -p T3 --buffer 50.

docs.title: Licence and data
docs.text: verdance is released under the MIT licence. The data it downloads keeps its own licence — notably GlobalBuildingAtlas heights (gba) are CC BY-NC 4.0 and FABDEM terrain is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, both non-commercial only; every source's licence is listed under data sources. The bundled map viewer includes MapLibre GL JS (BSD-3-Clause).

docs.title: Modules
docs.text: Process What it computes Output (one CSV per geo code) Trees Segments individual tree crowns from a canopy height model (local CHM tiles or the global Meta/WRI 1 m CHM) into data.trees_dir, for T3/Tree_count/Visibility trees_<geo_code>.parquet: treeID, height, area, top_x, top_y, crown geometry T3 Trees (height and area strictly above --tree_height/--tree_area) whose centroid lies within --buffer metres of each building building_id, tree_count_<buffer>m, sub-geo code T30 Canopy cover % per sub-geo unit, from CHM raster tiles, the Meta canopy height model on AWS, a GEE canopy-height asset, or tree polygons sub-geo code, canopy_cover, total_pixels T30_buildings Canopy cover % within --buffer metres of each building (distributed Sedona RS_ZonalStats for raster sources), same canopy sources as T30 building_id, tree_pixels, total_pixels, canopy_cover T300 Road-network and Euclidean distance from each building to the nearest park building_id, distances, closest park ids, sub-geo code Tree_count Total tree count per sub-geo unit, each tree counted once in the unit containing its centroid (no size filter, unlike T3) sub-geo code, tree_count Heights A height for every building footprint from an ordered chain of sources (footprint attributes, GlobalBuildingAtlas, UT-GLOBUS, Open Buildings 2.5D Temporal, GHS-BUILT-H, local files) database/building_heights_<key>.parquet: building_height, height_source, height_quality Visibility (optional) Trees within --buffer metres that can be seen from some window of each building, with buildings and trees blocking the view building_id, visible_trees, visible_trees_ground, candidate_trees, n_floors, building_height, height_source, sub-geo code Spectral (optional) Spectral indices (NDVI, NDWI, …) per sub-geo unit via Google Earth Engine: a per-pixel temporal composite over the date range (--composite max, the default, or median), then the spatial median over each unit sub-geo code, one column per index Merge Evaluates the 3-30-300 rule per building and consolidates all module outputs into database/T3_30_300_spectral.parquet one row per geo unit (see Merge)

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Run one module at a time; Merge last. verdance run --help lists every option.

verdance run -c config.yaml -p Trees      # optional: segment trees from a CHM into trees_dir
verdance run -c config.yaml -p T3 --buffer 100
verdance run -c config.yaml -p T30
verdance run -c config.yaml -p T30_buildings --buffer 100
verdance run -c config.yaml -p T300
verdance run -c config.yaml -p Tree_count
verdance run -c config.yaml -p Heights         # building heights (Visibility builds them if missing)
verdance run -c config.yaml -p Visibility --buffer 50   # optional: trees in view
verdance run -c config.yaml -p Spectral        # optional, needs GEE
verdance run -c config.yaml -p Merge
verdance viz -c config.yaml                    # interactive map, see [Visualising results](visualising.md)

Useful options:

  • --geo_level / --sub_geo_level — which levels of columns.geo_levels to iterate over / aggregate to (defaults: coarsest / finest); Merge's --geo_level defaults to the second-finest level instead
  • --dggs h3|s2|geohash|a5|rhealpix --dggs_resolution N — aggregate to grid cells instead of the finest census level (also settable as dggs/dggs_resolution in the config). Grid runs sit beside census-unit runs: T30, Tree_count and Merge write grid-suffixed outputs (T30_h3_9/, database/T3_30_300_spectral_h3_9.parquet), and the per-building modules (T3, T300, …) need not be re-run — Merge aggregates them through the grid's buildings overlay. With a grid, the rule's "30" uses each building's cell canopy. To add H3 res 9 to an existing run: -p T30, -p Tree_count and -p Merge, each with --dggs h3 --dggs_resolution 9
  • --geo_code CODE — process a single geography instead of all
  • --parallel --n_workers 4 — process geo codes concurrently (per-geo Spark views are isolated, so results match sequential runs)
  • --no-overwrite — skip geo codes whose output CSV already exists (resume an interrupted run)
  • --query_method sql|rdd — Sedona join strategy for T3 (default sql). sql uses an indexed spatial join and returns a row for every building, with tree_count 0 where no tree is in range; rdd omits those buildings (Merge zero-fills them, so merged totals match, but its per-geo CSVs are incomplete on their own). On the London region (2.83M buildings × 2.58M trees) sql took 47 s against 74 s for rdd
  • --tree_area / --tree_height — a tree counts in T3 and Visibility only if its canopy area (m²) and height (m) are strictly greater than these (defaults 10 and 3)
  • --vis_engine raster|vector — Visibility engine (default visibility.engine, i.e. raster; see Tree visibility)
  • --low_threshold / --high_threshold — canopy-height band in metres for T30/T30_buildings binarisation (default 3–60)
  • --gee_scale — download resolution in metres for the T30/T30_buildings GEE canopy source (default 1.0; raise to e.g. 10 for faster, lighter downloads over large regions — canopy is still thresholded at native resolution and each coarse pixel stores its canopy fraction, so cover stays unbiased)
  • --composite max|median — Spectral temporal composite (default max)
  • --rule_t3_buffer, --rule_t3_metric, --rule_t30_buffer, --rule_distance — how Merge evaluates the rule per building (see Merge)

docs.title: Canopy cover source (T30, T30_buildings)
docs.text:
T30 and T30_buildings pick their canopy source by what's configured, in priority order:

  1. CHM raster tiles (chm_tiles_dir) — local .tif tiles, binarised to a canopy/no-canopy mask between --low_threshold and --high_threshold metres.
  2. Meta/WRI canopy height from AWS (meta_chm: v1 or v2) — the tiles covering the area are downloaded once from Meta's public bucket into the CHM cache (data.chm_cache_dir, else $VERDANCE_CACHE_DIR), cropped, binarised at native ~1 m resolution and reprojected to the config CRS; masks are cached under <base_dir>/database/meta_canopy/, named by geo code, release and height band.
data:
  meta_chm: v2
  • v1 — the original release (Tolan et al. 2024; forests/v1/alsgedi_global_v6_float, zoom-9 tiles of ~150–400 MB). The same data as the GEE asset below: over a 600 m Cambridge square, v1 from AWS gives 7.63 % cover and v1 through GEE 7.62 %. Like v2, v1 tiles declare no nodata — but v1 ships no imagery footprints, so there is nothing to mask with: unimaged pixels read 0 and count as mapped-but-treeless, which deflates cover wherever imagery is missing inside a unit (open water, gaps). Prefer v2 where that matters.
  • v2 — forests/v2/global/dinov3_global_chm_v2_ml3 (zoom-10 tiles of ~20–250 MB, heights in whole metres). The same Cambridge square gives 12.78 %, so v1 and v2 results are not interchangeable. v2 tiles declare no nodata, so unimaged pixels (e.g. open sea) read 0 like bare ground; verdance masks pixels outside each tile's imagery footprints (metadata/<quadkey>.geojson) as nodata on download and keeps the footprints beside the tile. Footprints can include near-shore sea, which then still counts as no canopy — mostly relevant for T30_buildings buffers on the coast, since census units are usually clipped to the coastline. Imagery dates differ by area (e.g. 2011–2018 in one Norfolk tile); each run logs the range for the area it reads.

Both releases are tiled in EPSG:3857 at 1.1943 units/pixel, so the ground sampling is 1.1943 × cos(latitude) m — about 0.74 m at Cambridge's 52°N but 1.19 m near the equator. Cover itself stays unbiased (tiles are binarised at native resolution, then reprojected to the config's metric CRS, so the counted pixels are equal-area), but the same config resolves narrow crowns better at higher latitudes — worth keeping in mind when comparing cities at very different latitudes.

meta_chm also selects the release wherever the meta CHM source is read (tree_segmentation.source: meta, raster Visibility); unset, those use v1. 3. GEE canopy-height asset (canopy_height_ee_path) — binarised server-side in Google Earth Engine and downloaded with xee; no local canopy data required. Needs gee_project in the config. Example asset (global 1 m Meta/WRI canopy height):

data:
  canopy_height_ee_path: projects/sat-io/open-datasets/facebook/meta-canopy-height
gee_project: my-gee-project

Downloaded rasters are cached under <base_dir>/database/gee_canopy/, named by geo code, height band and scale. At the native 1 m scale large regions can be slow — use --gee_scale 10 to trade detail for speed: the mask is binarised at the native 1 m and averaged to canopy fraction per 10 m pixel server-side, so cover estimates stay consistent with 1 m runs. 4. Tree polygons (trees_dir) — canopy cover as the area of the union of crowns clipped to each unit / unit area (a crown straddling two units counts only its own part in each; overlapping crowns are not double-counted); used when no raster or GEE source is set. Point trees fall back to their tree_area attribute.

Where T30 reports canopy per sub-geo unit, T30_buildings reports it per building, within --buffer metres of each footprint (--buffer 0 for the footprint alone). Raster sources run distributed through Sedona (RS_TileExplode + RS_ZonalStats), so large CHM tile sets scale across Spark workers; the vector source uses an ST_Intersection area ratio. CHM nodata pixels are excluded from total_pixels in both modules. Where CHM tiles overlap (e.g. several survey years), data.chm_overlap decides which heights are used — latest (default; the last path in sorted order, i.e. the latest year for <dir>/<year>/ layouts) or max (per-pixel maximum) — in T30, T30_buildings and Trees alike; T30_buildings first composites overlapping tiles into non-overlapping chunks under the CHM cache, since it sums pixel counts per tile. One difference to keep in mind: T30_buildings counts every pixel touching a buffer while T30 counts pixels whose centre falls in the unit. CHM tiles are searched recursively under chm_tiles_dir, matching data.chm_pattern (default *.tif); Defra VOM hillshades (VOM_HS_*, stored beside every height tile) are always skipped. In Merge, per-building canopy is averaged up to the geo level as building_canopy_cover_<buffer>m (included automatically when T30_buildings output exists).

docs.title: Tree segmentation (Trees)
docs.text:
Trees derives the crowns T3 counts from a canopy height model, so the "3" can be measured anywhere a CHM exists:

verdance run -c config.yaml -p Trees --parallel --n_workers 32   # writes data.trees_dir/trees_<geo_code>.parquet
verdance run -c config.yaml -p T3 --buffer 50

The CHM is smoothed, treetops are found with a height-dependent circular local-maximum window, and crowns are grown from them with Dalponte & Coomes (2016) region growing — a numpy/scipy port of the lidR pipeline used for the Defra VOM trees (preset: legacy_vom reproduces it: ~99.7 % of crowns match lidR one-to-one, at ~6× lidR's speed on one core). Large areas are processed in blocks with a halo, in parallel; a tree belongs to the block and geo code containing its treetop, so blocks and neighbouring geo codes never duplicate or cut trees.

Sources (tree_segmentation.source): chm_tiles mosaics the tiles under data.chm_tiles_dir — where tiles overlap, e.g. several survey years, data.chm_overlap: latest keeps the last path in sorted order (the latest year for <dir>/<year>/ layouts) and max takes the per-pixel maximum across them, so a tree seen in any survey counts (in London, Defra's December 2020 VOM shows canopy at 36–49 % of surveyed street trees vs 49–77 % in 2018; max raised the share of inventory trees visible in the CHM from 52 % to 77 %); meta downloads the Meta/WRI global canopy height tiles covering the area from AWS (release set by data.meta_chm, default v1: ~240 MB per zoom-9 tile; v2: ~20–250 MB per zoom-10 tile; cached) and segments them on their native grid, with lengths converted to ground metres.

Presets (tree_segmentation.preset, individual values overridable under params) were tuned with scripts/tune_tree_segmentation.py, scoring only trees T3 would count (crown > 10 m², height > 3 m) against the London borough tree inventory (recall on surveyed trees visible in the CHM; precision inside surveyed crowns, since council inventories omit private trees) and NeonTreeEvaluation (full precision/recall), with London boroughs split into tuning and held-out sets. Held-out results:

Preset CHM London F1 London recall NEON precision / recall legacy_vom Defra VOM (chm_overlap: max) 0.48 0.32 0.84 / 0.19 vom Defra VOM (chm_overlap: max) 0.58 0.46 0.87 / 0.46 legacy_vom Meta 0.41 0.33 — meta Meta 0.48 0.43 —

On an independent check — Cambridge City Council's 2024 inventory (20,779 trees, not used in tuning; scripts/evaluate_trees_survey.py) — vom raised the share of surveyed trees matched within 3 m from 34 % to 46 % (F1 0.56 → 0.68), while meta matched 23 %, little better than legacy_vom on Meta: the gain on Meta did not transfer beyond London.

Meta's smoother, whole-metre heights still split about one surveyed crown in two, so expect its T3 counts to run higher than LiDAR's (over Cambridge: 147k vs 120k T3-eligible trees with the tuned presets).

docs.title: Building heights (Heights)
docs.text:
Visibility needs a height for every building. Heights attaches one from an ordered chain of sources — for each building the first source with a valid height wins (heights.min_height–heights.max_height, default 2–300 m), and buildings no source covers get heights.default_height (6 m), flagged height_source: default, so they still block views:

heights:
  sources:                      # first valid height wins
    - native                    # the footprints' own height (Overture, OSM, columns.building_height_col),
                                #   else floor count x storey_height (num_floors, or options levels_col)
    - gba                       # GlobalBuildingAtlas polygons
    - {source: utglobus, city: bogota}
    - {source: open_buildings_temporal, year: 2023}
    - ghs_built_h               # coarse global fallback
    - {source: file, path: /data/ndsm.tif, stat: median, name: lidar}
  default_height: 6.0
  storey_height: 3.0            # metres per floor, also Visibility's floor spacing
  min_overlap: 0.3              # vector sources: share of the footprint they must cover

The sources themselves, with their coverage and licences, are listed under data sources.

Vector sources lend each footprint the area-weighted height of the source polygons covering it (so a block the source splits into several buildings still matches), when they cover at least min_overlap of it. Raster sources give the median (GHS: mean) of the pixels whose centre lies inside the footprint, or of every touched pixel for footprints smaller than a pixel; GHS cells are sampled on a 10 m grid so the mean approximates an area-weighted mean. Remote sources come through Google Earth Engine (gee_project) and are cached under the CHM cache directory (data.chm_cache_dir, else $VERDANCE_CACHE_DIR): rasters as tiles aligned to a fixed grid, polygons as small lon/lat chunks, so reruns and neighbouring study areas reuse them. Each source's heights are cached per source (database/heights/), and the combined table is database/building_heights_<key>.parquet, keyed by the chain and the buildings cache — a new chain builds a new table rather than reusing a stale one. The run logs the share of buildings each source supplied.

scripts/evaluate_heights.py compares the cached sources against reference heights. Against Verisk heights in Cambridge (45,719 buildings; --levels_col premise_floor_count):

Source Coverage MAE (m) Bias (m) Spearman ghs_built_h 95 % 3.3 −2.9 0.29 gba 89 % 4.1 −3.9 0.38 floor count × 3 m 99 % 2.6 −2.5 0.30

Both global datasets run 3–4 m below Verisk, whose two-storey median of 8.9 m suggests it measures to the roof ridge, and rank buildings only weakly. Over Bogotá's 2.17 M Overture footprints the chain above took heights from GBA for 81 %, Open Buildings Temporal 10 %, GHS-BUILT-H 4 %, UT-GLOBUS 1 % and Overture 0.1 %, leaving 4 % at the default (16 min, 8 GB peak memory).

docs.title: Tree visibility (Visibility, optional)
docs.text:
Where T3 counts trees near a building, Visibility counts the ones that can be seen from it. It looks from the windows: observer points every visibility.facade_spacing metres (5) around each footprint, facade_offset (0.5 m) outside the wall, at the eye height of every floor (floor i: i × heights.storey_height + eye_height, 1.5 m up; at least one floor). Walls shared with a neighbour (terraced houses) have no windows. It looks at each tree's treetop (top_x, top_y from Trees, else a point inside the crown) and crown_points (4) points on its crown at crown_point_height (2/3) of its height. A tree is visible when some window sees some target point over every obstacle — every building, the observer's own included, at its Heights height, and the vegetation — as flat-topped prisms on flat ground (grazing contact blocks). Inside the target tree's own crown only buildings block, so a tree never hides itself, nor do crowns overlapping it. The candidates are the trees T3 counts — centroid within --buffer m, above --tree_area/--tree_height — with the distance measured exactly, whereas T3's polygonal ST_Buffer trims up to ~2 % of the radius at the corners, so candidate_trees can exceed tree_count_<b>m by a tree or two (3 % of Bogotá's buildings at 50 m, 11 % at 100 m). Smaller trees still block views.

Since visibility only improves with height, each building–tree pair reduces to the lowest eye height from which the tree is visible. Per building the output has visible_trees (seen from some floor), visible_trees_ground (from the ground floor), candidate_trees (T3's count), n_floors, building_height and height_source.

Two engines share these definitions:

  • raster (default) — casts the sightlines over a surface model on a visibility.resolution grid (1 m): buildings burned at their heights plus the vegetation, which is the canopy height model when one is configured (data.chm_tiles_dir or tree_segmentation.source; Meta's CHM is cleared on roofs, mask_chm_buildings) and the tree crowns at their heights otherwise (vegetation: auto|chm|crowns). A numba kernel visits every pixel each sightline crosses, in parallel (--parallel --n_workers N sets the threads, default 16); buildings are processed in tile_size tiles (2 km). It needs no Spark. Edges are only as sharp as the grid: a sightline that clips a building corner by less than a pixel may be judged differently from exact geometry (set resolution: 0.5 to tighten).
  • vector (--vis_engine vector) — the exact computation in Sedona SQL, intersecting every sightline with every footprint and crown polygon; a reference for small areas, writing Visibility_vector/ so Merge never mixes engines. On the synthetic city both engines agree on 47 of 48 buildings (the other differs by one ground-floor tree, a sightline grazing a building corner); on three Cambridge output areas (312 buildings) they agree on meets_3 for 99.7 % of buildings, with the raster engine seeing 2.5 % fewer trees on average, at ~1 s per area against ~50 s.

Building heights come from the Heights chain (built on the first Visibility run when missing) and tree heights from tree_height_col. Visibility needs crowns in data.trees_dir, and by default reads terrain from Earth Engine (below): set terrain.source: null for flat ground without GEE.

Terrain. The raster engine stands everything on the ground: buildings sit flat at the ground under their representative point plus their height, vegetation on the ground, windows and targets on the ground under them (floors stay relative to it), and the bare ground itself — a hill, a ridge — blocks sightlines. The ground comes from terrain.source:

terrain:
  source: fabdem      # fabdem (default) | copernicus | nasadem | /path/to/dtm.tif or directory | null (flat)
  resolution: 30      # GEE download resolution (m), resampled bilinearly onto the visibility grid

The terrain sources and their licences are listed under data sources.

Use a bare-earth model: surface models already contain rooftops and canopy in cities, so building and tree heights would be counted twice (in central Bogotá Copernicus reads 8 m above FABDEM). DEM tiles are cached under the CHM cache directory. The vector engine always assumes flat ground. In Cambridge (flat) terrain changed the visible-tree count of 1.2 % of buildings and meets_3 for 12 of 45,682.

Study-area edges. context_buffer (default 100 m, a top-level key; 0 disables) gathers context in a ring around the study area, so edge buildings are judged like any other:

  • Buildings — with a remote building source (osm, overture, open_buildings) the ring's footprints are fetched once into database/context_buildings.parquet. They get heights from the Heights chain and block views, but belong to no unit, so they are never observers and appear in no output. A building file is used whole, so extend it past the study area to cover the ring.
  • Trees — a full -p Trees run also segments the ring into trees_context.parquet (--geo_code context does only the ring, e.g. for an existing run), so trees just across the boundary count for edge buildings in T3 and Visibility; Tree_count and T30 still count only trees inside each unit. A tree file is used whole.
  • The canopy height model and the DEM are read past the boundary anyway.

First results (raster engine, 16 threads):

Study area Buffer Run time Candidates Visible (ground floor) Meets 3: proximity → visibility Cambridge — 45,682 buildings, Verisk heights, VOM crowns 50 m 1.5 min 16.9 11.0 (9.9) 96.9 % → 92.2 % 100 m 1.8 min 62.8 21.9 (17.1) 99.5 % → 97.2 % Cambridge, GBA heights instead 50 m 1.6 min 16.9 10.8 (10.3) 96.9 % → 93.0 % Bogotá — 2.17 M buildings, global heights, Meta CHM 50 m 8 min 4.7 1.2 (1.0) 28.9 % → 10.7 % 100 m 9 min 20.9 2.8 (2.1) 60.7 % → 17.5 %

These runs used flat ground and no context ring. With FABDEM terrain and the 100 m ring (210 k ring trees, 10.6 k ring buildings), Bogotá took 13 min per buffer; the share meeting the 3 by visibility barely moved (10.7 % → 10.7 % at 50 m, 17.5 % → 17.6 % at 100 m) — most of the city sits on the flat Sabana — but terrain changed the visible-tree count of 27–34 % of buildings on the eastern hillsides (Chapinero, La Candelaria, Santa Fe) against 6–8 % on the plain, and the ring added candidates for 0.3 % (50 m) and 0.9 % (100 m) of buildings. Rerunning T3 with the ring trees raised the count of 6,328 edge buildings at 50 m (the share meeting the 3 by proximity went from 28.9 % to 29.0 %). After Merge, 0.2 % of Bogotá's buildings meet 3-30-300 with 3 = trees nearby and 0.1 % with 3 = trees in view — the 30 is the binding criterion (0.3 % of buildings have 30 % canopy within 100 m) — and per UPZ 21–36 % of the trees within 50 m of a building are in view from it (10–19 % within 100 m). Peak memory was 0.6 GB (Cambridge) and 4.3 GB (Bogotá). Swapping Verisk for GBA heights in Cambridge changed meets_3 for 1.6 % of buildings. Where vegetation comes from the CHM, every canopy pixel blocks — street trees hide each other — so a smaller share of the candidates is visible than with crown polygons.

docs.title: Merge and the 3-30-300 rule
docs.text:
Merge accepts --t3_buffers, repeated once per buffer (e.g. --t3_buffers 50 --t3_buffers 100; default 10, 25, 50, 75 and 100), and combines whichever T3 buffer runs exist; Spectral, T30_buildings and Visibility outputs are included only if present. It aggregates to --geo_level, which for Merge defaults to the second-finest level of columns.geo_levels (the finest with a DGGS), reading sub-geo results at --sub_geo_level (default: finest).

Per unit it reports means — tree_count_<b>m, canopy_cover (area-weighted), park_distance_manhattan (road network) and park_distance_euclidean, plus building_canopy_cover_<b>m, visible_trees_<b>m and visible_trees_ground_<b>m when available — and total_trees. With Visibility it also reports share_visible_<b>m: the % of the unit's building–tree pairs within the buffer where the tree is in view (Σ visible ÷ Σ candidates).

Because the rule is a test every home should pass, Merge also evaluates it per building and writes database/T3_30_300_buildings.parquet with meets_3, meets_30, meets_300 and meets_3_30_300. The per-unit table gains pct_meets_3, pct_meets_30, pct_meets_300 and pct_meets_3_30_300 (% of buildings passing):

  • 3 — at least 3 trees within --rule_t3_buffer metres (default 50): counted by T3 (--rule_t3_metric proximity, the default) or visible from some floor (--rule_t3_metric visibility, needs Visibility at that buffer). Whenever both outputs exist the table keeps meets_3_proximity and meets_3_visibility beside meets_3, and the combined rule under each, meets_3_30_300_proximity and meets_3_30_300_visibility (with pct_ of all four per unit), and the parquet's verdance_rule metadata records which metric and columns the rule used
  • 30 — canopy cover of the building's sub-geo unit (the neighbourhood reading of the rule) is ≥ 30 %; with --rule_t30_buffer N, T30_buildings canopy within N metres of the building instead
  • 300 — distance to the nearest park is ≤ 300 m, straight-line by default (--rule_distance euclidean, as in the WHO guideline) or network

A criterion with missing input is left null and excluded from that percentage; the combined rule is only evaluated where all three are known. T3 and Visibility counts are proxies for "seeing" trees: T3 counts trees near the building, Visibility checks line of sight.

docs.title: Per-building outputs
docs.text: Each building belongs to exactly one census unit — the one containing its representative point — and is output only by that unit's run, including buildings that straddle unit boundaries. Buildings whose representative point lies outside every unit are skipped. T3's default sql query path returns a row for every building, with tree_count 0 where no tree is in the buffer; --query_method rdd omits those buildings instead, and Merge fills them with 0. T300 keeps every building: with no reachable park within osm.fetch_buffer (default 2 km) its distances are null.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
A study area is described by one YAML file. The smallest useful config needs only census boundaries of your own — one polygon per unit, with a column for each level of the hierarchy — and takes everything else from global open data:

# mycity.yaml
study_area_name: MyCity
crs: EPSG:32630                   # a projected CRS in metres covering the city (e.g. its UTM zone)

data:
  census_boundaries: /path/to/wards.gpkg   # one polygon per unit, e.g. columns district_code, ward_code
  buildings: overture             # Overture Maps footprints
  parks_sites: overture           # Overture parks and recreation grounds
  parks_access: osm               # OSM entrances, else where park boundaries meet roads
  roads: osm                      # OSM walking network
  meta_chm: v1                    # Meta/WRI 1 m canopy height from AWS: the "30"
  trees_dir: /path/to/output/trees   # filled by `-p Trees` below: the "3"

tree_segmentation:
  source: meta                    # segment the trees from the same canopy height model
  preset: meta

park_min_area_ha: 0.5             # ignore green spaces under 0.5 ha (WHO guidance)
terrain:
  source: null                    # flat ground for Visibility (the fabdem default needs GEE)

columns:
  geo_levels: [district_code, ward_code]   # coarsest → finest

output:
  base_dir: /path/to/output

Check it before committing to a long run:

verdance validate -c mycity.yaml

Then run the modules one at a time, Merge last, and open the map:

verdance run -c mycity.yaml -p Trees                  # segment tree crowns from the canopy height model
verdance run -c mycity.yaml -p T3 --buffer 50         # trees within 50 m of each building
verdance run -c mycity.yaml -p T30                    # canopy cover per ward
verdance run -c mycity.yaml -p T300                   # distance to the nearest park
verdance run -c mycity.yaml -p Tree_count
verdance run -c mycity.yaml -p Visibility --buffer 50 # optional: trees in view from the windows
verdance run -c mycity.yaml -p Merge --t3_buffers 50  # the rule per building and per unit
verdance viz -c mycity.yaml                           # interactive map at http://localhost:8765

The first run fetches the buildings, parks and roads once and caches them as parquet under <output.base_dir>/database/. The results are database/T3_30_300_buildings.parquet (one row per building, with meets_3, meets_30, meets_300 and meets_3_30_300) and database/T3_30_300_spectral.parquet (one row per unit, with the share of buildings meeting each criterion).

examples/generic.yaml documents every config key; download it with

curl -O https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sdgresearch/verdance/master/examples/generic.yaml

docs.title: Where files go
docs.text:
verdance writes nothing to the directory you run it from. Everything goes to the places below; on a shared machine or a small home directory, point the caches at a large disk.

What Default location Change it with Results, parquet cache of the inputs, viz.duckdb <output.base_dir>/ and <output.base_dir>/database/ output.base_dir in the config Logs (one file per module, plus viz.log) <output.base_dir>/logs/ — Downloads shared between runs: canopy-height tiles, Earth Engine rasters (heights, terrain, canopy), OpenStreetMap responses <output.base_dir>/database/chm_cache/ data.chm_cache_dir in the config, else the VERDANCE_CACHE_DIR environment variable Sedona/Spark jars (~110 MB, downloaded once) ~/.ivy2 VERDANCE_IVY_DIR DuckDB spatial extension for verdance viz (downloaded once) ~/.duckdb/extensions VERDANCE_DUCKDB_EXTENSIONS Temporary files: Spark shuffle and spill files, JVM temp files, Spark's warehouse directory the system temp directory TMPDIR (SPARK_LOCAL_DIRS overrides it for Spark's shuffle files) Earth Engine credentials ~/.config/earthengine/ earthengine authenticate

The environment variables themselves are listed under installation.

Rebuild the cache after changing inputs

The parquet cache under database/ is built once from the inputs. Delete <output.base_dir>/database/ after changing input files or column mappings so it is rebuilt.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• UnsupportedClassVersionError, or Spark fails to start — the Java on PATH / in JAVA_HOME is too old (< 11) or too new (> 17). Point JAVA_HOME at a Java 17.
  • Overpass server busy (HTTP 502) warnings — the public OpenStreetMap API is overloaded; verdance retries with growing waits (up to ~15 min). Responses that did arrive are cached, so rerunning later resumes.
  • The JVM runs out of memory (OutOfMemoryError, Java heap space) — raise SPARK_DRIVER_MEMORY, or process fewer units at once (drop --parallel, or a coarser --geo_level).
  • Results ignore changed inputs or column mappings — the parquet cache is reused; delete <output.base_dir>/database/.
  • Missing consolidated outputs for: [...] from Merge — run the listed modules first, with the same --dggs options (a grid Merge needs T30 and Tree_count at that grid).
  • Home directory full — move the caches with VERDANCE_CACHE_DIR, VERDANCE_IVY_DIR, VERDANCE_DUCKDB_EXTENSIONS and TMPDIR (see Where files go).

docs.title: Visualising results
docs.text:
verdance viz opens an interactive map of whatever has been computed so far:

verdance viz -c config.yaml            # opens http://localhost:8765

All controls sit in a sidebar on the left, split into Map (basemap, parks, trees, boundary lines), Buildings (one value per footprint) and Areas (one value per census unit or grid cell); a card in the top-right corner summarises the whole study area — buildings, trees, parks counted, canopy cover of the whole study area (total canopy ÷ total measured area, from T30), medians of the rule's inputs and the share of buildings meeting 3, 30, 300 and all three. When Merge kept both "3" metrics, the card shows the rule with 3 = trees nearby and with 3 = trees in view, the one --rule_t3_metric chose first.

  • Buildings are coloured by any per-building metric (T3 tree counts, park distances, T30_buildings canopy, Visibility's trees in view — from any floor, from the ground floor, and the share of nearby trees in view — building heights and, after Merge, the meets_* rule flags, including the rule under each "3" metric). Each coloured layer has its own palette (ColorBrewer, viridis, magma, cividis; reversible) and classes: quantile, equal interval, natural breaks (Jenks), logarithmic, continuous rank-stretched colour (every part of a skewed distribution gets contrast) or rule threshold, with 3–9 classes. The rule threshold uses diverging colours centred on the 3-30-300 threshold (3 trees, 30 %, 300 m). A rule flag is drawn as a gradient of the value it tests — trees within the rule buffer, the canopy the rule used, the park distance, or for the combined rule the number of criteria met (0–3, counting the "3" of that rule) — with its pass/fail counts in the legend; switch to plain pass/fail there.
  • Areas (every census level, plus any DGGS grid already built, e.g. "H3 res 9") can be filled with a unit metric — Merge's table at its level, T30/Tree_count/Spectral at the sub-geo level, and averages of the building metrics at every level — or outlined. Boundaries toggles outlines of any number of levels at once, e.g. ward borders over an H3 fill. Set columns.geo_level_labels / geo_level_names to show levels and units by name.
  • Parks shows the green spaces T300 counts (solid; at least park_min_area_ha) and the smaller ignored ones (dashed); click one for its name and area.
  • Trees from data.trees_dir are drawn to scale (crown radius from the area column or polygon area) or as dots when only points are available. Green is reserved for trees and purple for parks; the default metric ramps are blues, red–blue and orange–brown.
  • Drag across the legend histogram to show only a value range; click a feature for all of its values.
  • Basemaps (no API keys): none, OpenFreeMap Positron or Liberty, OpenStreetMap, Esri World Imagery (sub-metre in most cities; Esri attribution, and Esri's terms expect an ArcGIS account beyond light non-commercial use), or Sentinel-2 imagery (EOX, 10 m, non-commercial).

Merge is optional: module CSVs are read directly when its parquets are missing. The first start builds database/viz.duckdb (geometry reprojected and indexed, statistics precomputed), and later starts reuse it until an output changes; --rebuild forces a rebuild and --no-trees skips the tree layer. Buildings and trees appear from zoom 14 (a view about 3.5 km across), which keeps whole-city datasets responsive; zoomed further out, show units instead.

The server listens on 127.0.0.1 only. On a remote machine, forward the port (ssh -L 8765:localhost:8765 host) and pass --no-browser. DuckDB downloads its spatial extension on first use; set VERDANCE_DUCKDB_EXTENSIONS=/some/dir if your home directory is full or read-only.

docs.title: Output layout
docs.text:
<output.base_dir>/
├── T3/            T3_<code>_<buffer>m.csv
├── T30/           T30_<code>.csv
├── T30_buildings/ T30_buildings_<code>_<buffer>m.csv
├── T300/          T300_<code>.csv
├── Tree_count/    Tree_count_<code>.csv
├── Visibility/    Visibility_<code>_<buffer>m.csv (Visibility_vector/ with --vis_engine vector)
├── Spectral/      Spectral_<code>.csv
├── logs/          <module>_processing.log, viz.log
├── T30_h3_9/, Tree_count_h3_9/   same, per grid cell (runs with --dggs h3 --dggs_resolution 9)
└── database/      parquet cache + consolidated outputs
    ├── chm_cache/                   ← download cache (unless data.chm_cache_dir or VERDANCE_CACHE_DIR is set)
    ├── building_heights_<key>.parquet ← one height per building (Heights; per-source caches in heights/)
    ├── context_buildings.parquet    ← footprints in the context_buffer ring (remote building sources)
    ├── T3_30_300_buildings.parquet  ← per-building 3-30-300 evaluation
    ├── T3_30_300_spectral.parquet   ← final merged table
    ├── h3_boundaries_res9.parquet   ← grid cells (+ T3_30_300_*_h3_9.parquet from a grid Merge)
    └── viz.duckdb                   ← map store built by `verdance viz`

docs.title: API reference
docs.text:
verdance is usable as a library as well as a command line tool. Three names are importable directly from the top-level package:

import verdance

cfg = verdance.load_config("mycity.yaml")
verdance.run(cfg, "T3", buffer=50)      # writes T3 CSVs, returns {geo_code: DataFrame | None}
merged = verdance.run(cfg, "Merge")     # consolidates and returns the merged unit table

They are imported lazily, so import verdance — to read verdance.__version__, say — does not pull in PySpark and the rest of the stack.

VerdanceConfig is documented alongside the YAML keys it mirrors, in the config reference.

The per-geo-code analysis modules (T3, T30, T30_buildings, T300, Tree_count) and Merge are covered by run(). Trees, Heights, Spectral and the raster Visibility engine have bespoke setup and remain CLI-only for now.

docs.title: verdance.run
docs.text:
Run one verdance process programmatically and return its result.

config is a path or a loaded VerdanceConfig. process is one of T3, T30, T30_buildings, T300, Tree_count or Merge. A Spark session is created (and reused via getOrCreate) unless one is passed as sedona.

Merge returns the merged unit DataFrame; the per-geo modules write their CSVs, record a run manifest, and return {geo_code: DataFrame | None} (None for a region that failed). For Trees, Heights, Spectral and raster Visibility, use the verdance CLI.

Source code in src/verdance/api.py 
def run(
    config,
    process: str,
    *,
    sedona=None,
    geo_level: str | None = None,
    sub_geo_level: str | None = None,
    geo_code: str | None = None,
    query_method: str = "sql",
    buffer: int = 100,
    tree_area: int = 10,
    tree_height: int = 3,
    low_threshold: int = 3,
    high_threshold: int = 60,
    gee_scale: float = 1.0,
    overwrite: bool = True,
    dggs: str | None = None,
    dggs_resolution: int | None = None,
    t3_buffers=(10, 25, 50, 75, 100),
    rule_t3_buffer: int = 50,
    rule_t30_buffer: int | None = None,
    rule_distance: str = "euclidean",
    rule_t3_metric: str = "proximity",
):
    """Run one verdance process programmatically and return its result.

    `config` is a path or a loaded `VerdanceConfig`. `process` is one of T3,
    T30, T30_buildings, T300, Tree_count or Merge. A Spark session is created
    (and reused via `getOrCreate`) unless one is passed as `sedona`.

    Merge returns the merged unit `DataFrame`; the per-geo modules write their
    CSVs, record a run manifest, and return `{geo_code: DataFrame | None}` (None
    for a region that failed). For Trees, Heights, Spectral and raster
    Visibility, use the `verdance` CLI.
    """
    if process != "Merge" and process not in PROCESS_FNS:
        raise NotImplementedError(
            f"verdance.run does not cover {process!r} — use the `verdance` CLI for Trees, Heights, "
            f"Spectral and raster Visibility. Programmatic processes: {sorted(PROCESS_FNS) + ['Merge']}."
        )

    cfg = config if isinstance(config, VerdanceConfig) else load_config(config)
    geo_levels = cfg.columns.geo_levels
    dggs = dggs if dggs is not None else cfg.dggs
    dggs_resolution = dggs_resolution if dggs_resolution is not None else cfg.dggs_resolution
    sedona = sedona or get_spark()

    if process == "Merge":
        from .merge import merge_output_csv, process_data

        t3b = list(t3_buffers)
        merge_output_csv(sedona, cfg, t3b, dggs=dggs, dggs_resolution=dggs_resolution)
        if dggs is not None:
            merge_geo = geo_level or sub_geo_level or get_system(dggs).column_name(dggs_resolution)
            merge_sub = sub_geo_level or get_system(dggs).column_name(dggs_resolution)
        else:
            merge_geo = geo_level or (geo_levels[-2] if len(geo_levels) > 1 else geo_levels[0])
            merge_sub = sub_geo_level or geo_levels[-1]
        return process_data(
            sedona, cfg, merge_geo, merge_sub, t3b, dggs=dggs, dggs_resolution=dggs_resolution,
            rule_t3_buffer=rule_t3_buffer, rule_t30_buffer=rule_t30_buffer,
            rule_distance=rule_distance, rule_t3_metric=rule_t3_metric,
        )

    # only T300 walks the road network and parks; the rest skip ~900 MB of reads
    tables = load_tables(sedona, cfg, dggs=dggs, dggs_resolution=dggs_resolution,
                         load_roads_parks=(process == "T300"))
    dirs = tables["output_dirs"]
    gl = geo_level or geo_levels[0]
    sgl = sub_geo_level or (geo_levels[-1] if len(geo_levels) > 1 else geo_levels[0])
    output_dir = dirs[_OUTPUT_DIR_KEY[process]]
    if dggs is not None:
        sgl = get_system(dggs).column_name(dggs_resolution)
        if process in ("T30", "Tree_count"):
            # grid runs sit beside the census-unit outputs instead of overwriting them
            output_dir = dirs["base"] / unit_output_name(process, dggs, dggs_resolution)
            output_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

    args_dict = {
        "sedona": sedona, "geo_level": gl, "sub_geo_level": sgl, "cfg": cfg, "output_dir": output_dir,
        "query_method": query_method, "buffer": buffer, "tree_area": tree_area, "tree_height": tree_height,
        "low_threshold": low_threshold, "high_threshold": high_threshold, "gee_scale": gee_scale,
        "overwrite": overwrite, "road_nodes_gdf": tables.get("road_nodes_gdf"),
        "road_edges_gdf": tables.get("road_edges_gdf"),
        # already filtered by load_tables; passing them keeps T300 from re-reading
        # and re-filtering the parks datasets once per geo code
        "parks_sites_gdf": tables.get("parks_sites_gdf"),
        "parks_access_gdf": tables.get("parks_access_gdf"),
    }
    codes = list([geo_code] if geo_code else tables["census_boundaries_gdf"][gl].unique())
    start = time.time()
    results, failed = {}, []
    for code in codes:
        try:
            result = run_process_code(process, args_dict, code)
        except Exception:
            logger.exception(f"{process}: error processing {code}")
            result = None
        results[code] = result
        if result is None:
            failed.append(code)
    write_run_manifest(
        output_dir, process, codes, [c for c in codes if c not in failed], failed,
        cfg=cfg, duration_s=time.time() - start,
        extra={"geo_level": gl, "sub_geo_level": sgl, "buffer": buffer},
    )
    return results

docs.title: verdance.load_config
docs.text:
Load and validate a verdance YAML config into a VerdanceConfig.

Unknown keys, missing required sections and a geographic crs are rejected here rather than part-way through a long Spark run.

Source code in src/verdance/config/loader.py 
def load_config(path: str | Path) -> VerdanceConfig:
    """Load and validate a verdance YAML config into a `VerdanceConfig`.

    Unknown keys, missing required sections and a geographic `crs` are rejected
    here rather than part-way through a long Spark run.
    """
    with open(path) as f:
        raw = yaml.safe_load(f)

    if not isinstance(raw, dict):
        kind = "empty" if raw is None else f"a {type(raw).__name__}"
        raise ValueError(f"Config file {path} is {kind}; expected a YAML mapping of settings")

    _require(raw, "study_area_name", "crs", "data", "columns", "output")
    _reject_unknown(raw, {f.name for f in fields(VerdanceConfig)}, "top-level config")

    data_raw = raw["data"]
    _require_section(data_raw, "data", "buildings", "parks_sites", "parks_access", "roads", "census_boundaries")
    _reject_unknown(data_raw, {f.name for f in fields(DataPaths)}, "data")

    columns_raw = raw["columns"]
    _require_section(columns_raw, "columns", "geo_levels")
    _reject_unknown(columns_raw, {f.name for f in fields(ColumnMapping)}, "columns")
    if not columns_raw.get("geo_levels"):
        raise ValueError("columns.geo_levels must be a non-empty list")
    if building_source(data_raw["buildings"]) is None and not columns_raw.get("building_id"):
        raise ValueError("columns.building_id is required when data.buildings is a file path")

    _validate_osm_sources(data_raw, columns_raw)
    osm_cfg = _parse_osm_section(raw.get("osm") or {})
    open_buildings_cfg = _parse_open_buildings_section(raw.get("open_buildings") or {})
    overture_cfg = _parse_overture_section(raw.get("overture") or {})
    tree_seg_cfg = _parse_tree_segmentation_section(raw.get("tree_segmentation") or {})
    heights_cfg = _parse_heights_section(raw.get("heights") or {})
    visibility_cfg = _parse_visibility_section(raw.get("visibility") or {})
    terrain_cfg = _parse_terrain_section(raw["terrain"] if "terrain" in raw else {})
    context_buffer = raw.get("context_buffer", 100.0)
    if isinstance(context_buffer, bool) or not isinstance(context_buffer, (int, float)) or context_buffer < 0:
        raise ValueError(f"context_buffer must be a non-negative number (metres), got {context_buffer!r}")

    output_raw = raw["output"]
    _require_section(output_raw, "output", "base_dir")
    _reject_unknown(output_raw, {f.name for f in fields(OutputPaths)}, "output")

    tile_raw = raw.get("tile_system", {})

    try:
        from pyproj import CRS
        crs_obj = CRS.from_user_input(raw["crs"])
    except Exception as e:
        raise ValueError(f"Invalid CRS '{raw['crs']}': {e}")
    if crs_obj.is_geographic:
        raise ValueError(
            f"crs '{raw['crs']}' is geographic (degrees). verdance measures areas in m² and buffers in "
            "metres, so a projected/metric CRS is required — e.g. the local UTM zone or a national grid."
        )

    dggs, dggs_resolution = _parse_dggs(raw)

    return VerdanceConfig(
        study_area_name=raw["study_area_name"],
        crs=raw["crs"],
        data=DataPaths(
            buildings=data_raw["buildings"],
            parks_sites=data_raw["parks_sites"],
            parks_access=data_raw["parks_access"],
            roads=data_raw["roads"],
            census_boundaries=data_raw["census_boundaries"],
            road_nodes=data_raw.get("road_nodes"),
            trees_dir=data_raw.get("trees_dir"),
            chm_tiles_dir=data_raw.get("chm_tiles_dir"),
            chm_pattern=data_raw.get("chm_pattern") or "*.tif",
            chm_overlap=_parse_chm_overlap(data_raw.get("chm_overlap")),
            chm_cache_dir=data_raw.get("chm_cache_dir"),
            canopy_height_ee_path=data_raw.get("canopy_height_ee_path"),
            meta_chm=_parse_meta_chm(data_raw.get("meta_chm")),
        ),
        columns=ColumnMapping(
            building_id=columns_raw.get("building_id"),
            building_layer=columns_raw.get("building_layer"),
            building_height_col=columns_raw.get("building_height_col"),
            building_use_col=columns_raw.get("building_use_col"),
            building_use_value=columns_raw.get("building_use_value"),
            road_node_id=columns_raw.get("road_node_id", "id"),
            road_edge_start=columns_raw.get("road_edge_start", "start_node"),
            road_edge_end=columns_raw.get("road_edge_end", "end_node"),
            road_edge_length=columns_raw.get("road_edge_length", "length"),
            road_edge_layer=columns_raw.get("road_edge_layer", "road_link"),
            road_node_layer=columns_raw.get("road_node_layer", "road_node"),
            park_id=columns_raw.get("park_id", "id"),
            park_function_col=columns_raw.get("park_function_col"),
            park_function_value=columns_raw.get("park_function_value"),
            park_access_ref_col=columns_raw.get("park_access_ref_col"),
            tree_height_col=columns_raw.get("tree_height_col", "height"),
            tree_area_col=columns_raw.get("tree_area_col", "area"),
            tree_id_col=columns_raw.get("tree_id_col", "treeID"),
            tree_layer=columns_raw.get("tree_layer", "trees"),
            geo_levels=columns_raw["geo_levels"],
            geo_level_labels=_level_mapping(columns_raw, "geo_level_labels"),
            geo_level_names=_level_mapping(columns_raw, "geo_level_names"),
        ),
        output=OutputPaths(base_dir=output_raw["base_dir"]),
        gee_project=raw.get("gee_project"),
        gee_boundaries_asset=raw.get("gee_boundaries_asset"),
        park_min_area_ha=_parse_park_min_area(raw.get("park_min_area_ha")),
        dggs=dggs,
        dggs_resolution=dggs_resolution,
        tile_system=TileSystemConfig(
            enabled=tile_raw.get("enabled", False),
            tile_name_pattern=tile_raw.get("tile_name_pattern"),
        ),
        osm=osm_cfg,
        overture=overture_cfg,
        open_buildings=open_buildings_cfg,
        tree_segmentation=tree_seg_cfg,
        heights=heights_cfg,
        visibility=visibility_cfg,
        terrain=terrain_cfg,
        context_buffer=float(context_buffer),
    )

docs.title: The rest of the package
docs.text:
The pages below document the internals, for extending verdance or calling a single stage directly.

  • Analysis modules — the T3, T30, T300 and Tree_count processes, and Merge
  • Pipeline — input loading, output layout and the DGGS backends
  • Data sources — OSM, Overture, Open Buildings, building heights, terrain
  • Optional modules — canopy sources, spectral indices, tree segmentation, visibility
  • Utilities — Spark/Sedona setup, caching, run manifests and the map viewer

docs.title: Analysis modules
docs.text: The per-geo-code processes that compute each part of the 3-30-300 rule, and the Merge step that consolidates them. Each module exposes a process_geo_code entry point, which verdance.run dispatches to.

docs.title: T3 — trees near each building
docs.text:
T3 — the "3" of the rule: trees within a buffer of each building.

Counts the tree crowns whose centroid falls within --buffer metres of each building, keeping only trees above the --tree_height and --tree_area thresholds, and writes one CSV per geo code.

docs.title: read_trees_unique(sedona, trees_dir, geo_boundary_gdf, cfg, geo_code, tree_area=10, tree_height=3)
docs.text:
Load trees for the geo_code boundary and register the geo_trees_<geo_code> view.

Reads either a single tree file or the files in trees_dir overlapping geo_boundary_gdf (pass it buffered by the building buffer so edge buildings see trees in neighbouring tiles). Columns are renamed to the canonical tree_height/tree_area names and reprojected to cfg.crs, then filtered (area > tree_area, height > tree_height, both strict) and reduced to centroids with a generated tree_id.

Source code in src/verdance/t3.py 
def read_trees_unique(
    sedona: SparkSession,
    trees_dir: Path,
    geo_boundary_gdf: gpd.GeoDataFrame,
    cfg: VerdanceConfig,
    geo_code: str,
    tree_area: int = 10,
    tree_height: int = 3,
) -> DataFrame:
    """Load trees for the geo_code boundary and register the `geo_trees_<geo_code>` view.

    Reads either a single tree file or the files in trees_dir overlapping
    geo_boundary_gdf (pass it buffered by the building buffer so edge
    buildings see trees in neighbouring tiles). Columns are renamed to the
    canonical tree_height/tree_area names and reprojected to cfg.crs, then
    filtered (area > tree_area, height > tree_height, both strict) and reduced
    to centroids with a generated tree_id.
    """
    logger.debug(f"Reading tree vector files for {geo_code}")

    geo_trees_gdf = load_trees_gdf(trees_dir, geo_boundary_gdf, cfg)

    geo_trees_sdf = sedona.createDataFrame(geo_trees_gdf)
    if "geom" in geo_trees_sdf.columns:
        geo_trees_sdf = geo_trees_sdf.withColumnRenamed("geom", "geometry")
    geo_trees_sdf = (
        geo_trees_sdf
        .where(f"tree_area > {tree_area} AND tree_height > {tree_height} AND geometry IS NOT NULL")
        .selectExpr("ST_Centroid(geometry) AS geometry", "tree_area", "tree_height")
        .withColumn("tree_id", monotonically_increasing_id())
    )
    geo_trees_sdf.createOrReplaceTempView(f"geo_trees_{view_suffix(geo_code)}")

    return geo_trees_sdf

docs.title: count_trees(sedona, geo_code)
docs.text:
Count trees per building buffer using a SQL spatial join.

Every building is returned, with tree_count 0 when its buffer holds no tree — but the counts come from an inner spatial join plus a zero-fill rather than one LEFT JOIN on ST_Intersects. Sedona cannot push a spatial index through an outer join, so the LEFT JOIN form degenerated into a nested loop over every building x tree pair (the same trap t30_buildings.get_canopy_cover_buildings_vector documents). Measured on one English district (46k buildings x 68k trees): the LEFT JOIN form took 1156 s, this form 3.4 s, and the RDD path 6.1 s; on the London region (2.83M x 2.58M) this form took 46.9 s and the RDD path 74.3 s. All agree on the tree total, and this form agrees row for row with the LEFT JOIN, while the RDD path omits buildings with no tree in range (4.5% of London).

Source code in src/verdance/t3.py 
def count_trees(sedona: SparkSession, geo_code: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Count trees per building buffer using a SQL spatial join.

    Every building is returned, with tree_count 0 when its buffer holds no
    tree — but the counts come from an inner spatial join plus a zero-fill
    rather than one LEFT JOIN on ST_Intersects. Sedona cannot push a spatial
    index through an outer join, so the LEFT JOIN form degenerated into a
    nested loop over every building x tree pair (the same trap
    t30_buildings.get_canopy_cover_buildings_vector documents). Measured on one
    English district (46k buildings x 68k trees): the LEFT JOIN form took
    1156 s, this form 3.4 s, and the RDD path 6.1 s; on the London region
    (2.83M x 2.58M) this form took 46.9 s and the RDD path 74.3 s. All agree on
    the tree total, and this form agrees row for row with the LEFT JOIN, while
    the RDD path omits buildings with no tree in range (4.5% of London).
    """
    sfx = view_suffix(geo_code)
    trees_within_buffer_sdf = sedona.sql(
        f"""
        SELECT b.building_id, COALESCE(c.tree_count, 0) AS tree_count
        FROM buildings_buffers_{sfx} b
        LEFT JOIN (
            SELECT bb.building_id, COUNT(*) AS tree_count
            FROM buildings_buffers_{sfx} bb, geo_trees_{sfx} t
            WHERE ST_Intersects(bb.geometry, t.geometry)
            GROUP BY bb.building_id
        ) c ON b.building_id = c.building_id
        """
    )
    return trees_within_buffer_sdf.toPandas()

docs.title: process_geo_code(sedona, query_method, geo_level, geo_code, sub_geo_level, cfg, output_dir, buffer=100, tree_area=10, tree_height=3, overwrite=True)
docs.text:
Compute T3 (trees within buffer metres of each building) for one geo_code.

Writes T3_<geo_code>_<buffer>m.csv to output_dir with columns building_id, tree_count_m, . Returns the DataFrame, the cached CSV when it exists and overwrite is False, or None on error. Source code in src/verdance/t3.py 

def process_geo_code(
    sedona: SparkSession,
    query_method: str,
    geo_level: str,
    geo_code: str,
    sub_geo_level: str,
    cfg: VerdanceConfig,
    output_dir: Path,
    buffer: int = 100,
    tree_area: int = 10,
